lead: Fault simulation asks how many modelled faults a vector set catches. ATPG, automatic test pattern generation, asks the reverse: for one undetected fault, what input vector exposes it at an output? The two programs form a loop. Fault simulation measures coverage after each vector; ATPG adds vectors for faults still missed. The loop ends when coverage reaches a target or no testable fault remains. Every fabricated chip then receives the compact set, so a manufacturing defect shows up as a wrong output instead of being shipped.
prereq: You need: fault collapsing from 6.2 and gate-level simulation from Unit 5.

blocks.text: A fault list is the collapsed set of modelled faults, such as line A stuck-at-0. Fault simulation applies one input vector to the good circuit and to every faulty circuit in the list. It records a fault as detected when at least one output differs between good and faulty machines.

The good circuit is simulated once. Faulty circuits can be simulated in parallel by packing 32 or 64 faults into the bits of a machine word. Deductive simulation evaluates good lines once and deduces faulty values. Concurrent simulation keeps an event list per fault. Speed matters because a large chip can have millions of collapsed faults and thousands of vectors.

blocks.where: C is fault coverage in percent, N_detected is the number of testable faults detected by the current vector set, and N_testable is the number of faults in the collapsed testable fault list.

blocks.text: Report coverage after each vector. Vectors that add no new detection are dropped; this is test compaction. Vector ordering can also reduce tester time, but it does not change final coverage.

sections.h3: ATPG methods, from exhaustive to algorithmic

blocks.text: Exhaustive ATPG applies all 2ⁿ vectors for n inputs. It is complete but impossible beyond small n. Pseudo-exhaustive testing partitions the circuit and exhausts small subcircuits. Random ATPG applies pseudo-random vectors; weighted random biases inputs toward values that activate faults. Algorithmic ATPG works backward from one fault.
In the D-algorithm, D means 1 in the good machine and 0 in the faulty machine. D-bar is the reverse: 0 in good, 1 in faulty. A line carrying D or D-bar is sensitized.

items: Fault activation: assign the faulty line the value that creates D or D-bar.
D-propagation: push D or D-bar toward an output through gates whose side inputs allow it.
Line justification: set the side inputs and primary inputs needed for each chosen gate.
Conflict and backtracking: if two requirements contradict, undo the last choice and try another.

blocks.text: The D-frontier is the set of gates with a D or D-bar on an input but no D or D-bar on the output. The J-frontier is the set of gates whose output is known but whose inputs are not yet justified. PODEM works on primary inputs and needs fewer backtracks. FAN uses fanout-free regions and multiple backtracks per pass.

sections.h3: Redundant faults, compaction and vector ordering

blocks.text: A redundant fault has no test: no input vector makes its effect reach an output. A stuck-at line that is logically redundant is the common case. An untestable fault has no test for another reason, such as an input tied off or a blocked path. Coverage is measured against the testable fault list, because counting redundant faults can make a 100 % target impossible.

Test compaction removes vectors that detect no new fault. Run fault simulation after each removal to confirm no fault is lost. Vector ordering puts high-coverage vectors first, or sorts by current demand when the tester and power grid need it. Compaction cuts test time and tester memory; ordering cuts test execution time and supply noise, not coverage.

The ATPG loop in the figure is therefore iterative: simulate, check coverage, generate for the undetected list, add vectors, simulate again. Stop at the target or when only redundant and untestable faults remain.

figure.caption: The loop measures coverage with fault simulation, then adds vectors for faults still undetected until the coverage target is met.

spec.title: The ATPG loop
spec.aria: Loop in which fault simulation measures coverage, and ATPG adds vectors for the still-undetected faults until the coverage target is reached.

examples.question: Question (6 marks): The circuit is Z = A·(B + C), built as G1 = NAND(A,B), G2 = NAND(A,C), Z = NAND(G1,G2). Use the D-algorithm to find a test for the fault A stuck-at-0. Show activation, propagation, the D-frontier and the final vector. State the good and faulty values of Z.
steps: Activation: for A stuck-at-0, set A = 1 in the good machine; the faulty line is fixed at 0. This puts D on A (good 1, faulty 0).
Propagate through G1 = NAND(A,B). Set B = 1 as a side input. Then G1 = NOT(A) for this input: good A=1 gives G1=0, faulty A=0 gives G1=1. So G1 carries D-bar (good 0, faulty 1).
G2 = NAND(A,C). Choose C = 0. Then G2 = 1 in both machines, because NAND(x,0)=1. G2 does not block the D-bar; it is a constant 1 side input to the last gate.
D-frontier: G1 now drives the Z gate with D-bar, while G2 is 1. Z = NAND(D-bar,1). In the good machine Z = NAND(0,1)=1; in the faulty machine Z = NAND(1,1)=0. So Z carries D.
Vector: (A,B,C) = (1,1,0). No line justification conflict occurred, so no backtracking was needed. The output difference Z = 1 good, Z = 0 faulty detects A stuck-at-0.
examples.answer: The test is (A,B,C) = (1,1,0); it gives Z = 1 in the good machine and Z = 0 in the faulty machine, so the fault is detected.
examples.check:
def nand(a, b):
    return 0 if (a == 1 and b == 1) else 1

A = 1
B = 1
C = 0
G1g = nand(A, B)
G2g = nand(A, C)
Zg = nand(G1g, G2g)
Af = 0
G1f = nand(Af, B)
G2f = nand(Af, C)
Zf = nand(G1f, G2f)
print(A)
print(B)
print(C)
print(Zg)
print(Zf)

traps: Reading D as 'the fault is present at this line' without the convention D = good 1, faulty 0; D-bar is good 0, faulty 1.
Forgetting that a redundant fault has no test, so 100 % coverage of all faults may be impossible; report coverage against the testable list.
Confusing the D-frontier, which propagates a difference, with the J-frontier, which justifies known values.
Calling a vector a test because it activates a fault, without checking that an output differs between good and faulty machines.
Counting all vectors applied as coverage, instead of detected testable faults divided by total testable faults.

quiz.q: Define D and D-bar in D-algorithm notation.
quiz.a: D = 1 in the good machine and 0 in the faulty machine. D-bar = 0 in good and 1 in faulty.
C = (N_detected ÷ N_testable) × 100%, where N_detected is detected testable faults and N_testable is total testable faults.

quiz.q: Why is the good circuit simulated only once in fault simulation?
quiz.a: Its line values are shared by all faulty copies; only faulty values differ, so one good simulation saves work when the fault list is large.

quiz.q: Why report coverage after each vector?
quiz.a: It shows which vectors add new detections; vectors with no new fault can be removed in compaction, and the loop can stop at the target.

quiz.q: In the worked example, after setting A=1 and B=1, what are G1 in the good and faulty machines? What symbol is on G1?
quiz.a: Good: G1 = NAND(1,1) = 0. Faulty: G1 = NAND(0,1) = 1. So G1 carries D-bar.

quiz.q: A collapsed testable fault list has 4,000 faults. Current vectors detect 3,600. Compute coverage.
A vector detects no new fault. Should it be kept? Explain in terms of compaction and fault simulation.
quiz.a: No, remove it; rerun fault simulation to confirm every fault it might have covered is covered by another vector. This is test compaction.

quiz.q: Why can 100% coverage of all faults be impossible even for a correct design?
quiz.a: Some faults are redundant or untestable and have no vector that makes an output differ; coverage is defined against the testable fault list, so an all-fault target may be below 100%.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial ATPG tools combine structural algorithms with SAT solvers and use fault simulation engines accelerated on GPUs. Cell-aware and layout-aware fault models add defects that classical stuck-at ATPG misses. Researchers study X-tolerant compaction and low-power ATPG, where vector ordering limits switching during scan shift. Search for 'cell-aware ATPG', 'X-filling', and 'SAT-based ATPG' to go further.
